entries.title: Merge the declared default into main, so the default can be flipped
entries.detail:
This repository's GitHub default is an agent's scratch branch. That is a
lie to every human and every tool that reads it, and `default-branch.mjs`
in flashy-infra runs daily to fix exactly this — but it refuses to switch
when the trunk is missing commits from the current default, because
flipping there leaves real work with nothing pointing at it.

That refusal was firing here. `main` was ahead in one direction and
behind in the other, so the nightly job could not act and the setting
stayed wrong.

Merging rather than resetting: a merge keeps every commit on both sides
and keeps anybody's checkout of the default branch valid. Nothing is
discarded and nothing is rewritten.

`main` is now a strict superset of the declared default, so the flip is
safe. Changing the setting itself is a repository permission and only
the owner can do it.

entries.title: Tell the estate the moment this repository pushes a record
entries.detail:
graph.yml in flashyos merges every property's fragment on a daily
schedule, so without a dispatch a change here is invisible to the estate
for up to 24 hours — and "the graph is a day behind" is
indistinguishable from "this property has nothing new to say".

The dispatch has been in the shiplog/backlog template since August and
in no repository, because each vendored its workflow before the template
had it. This adds it, gated on the commit step having actually pushed: a
dispatch per run rather than per change would turn one daily merge into
a merge per push across thirty repositories.

The commit step is replaced with one canonical form rather than patched,
because the estate had two vintages of it — some repositories carry a
five-attempt push retry the template lacked, and re-emitting would have
deleted it. Both halves are here now.

The retry resolves the branch per run instead of resetting to a literal
origin/main. Eleven repositories in this estate have an agent branch as
their default, and there a rejected push would reset the checkout to a
different branch and push that over the deploy branch.

Unset ESTATE_DISPATCH_TOKEN means a delay of up to 24 hours, never a
loss — the daily merge is the floor, and the step says so loudly rather
than skipping green.

Kind: feature

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FDosmV9fXV6oZ9NXe7PZ76

entries.title: Re-vendor shiplog: the filter learns directory/1, delivery/1 and intent/1
entries.detail:
Three formats gained a workflow that commits a refresh. Without this the
first run of each seals as work under agent/unattributed, inflating the
two numbers the record exists to make honest.

A vendored change does nothing until the copy is replaced, and a stale
copy does not fail — it disagrees, silently, about exactly the field
somebody has just changed.

Kind: chore

entries.title: Give this repository's directory fragment a machine that refreshes it
entries.detail:
shipped/1 and backlog/1 each ship a workflow with their adoption, so
every repository filing one has something re-running the emitter.
directory/1 never did — sixteen repositories in this estate got the
fragment and nothing else, and were still serving the bytes one
hand-sweep produced on 2026-08-31.

Nothing was red, and nothing would have gone red. A fragment nobody
re-emits does not decay for a year; it stops being true. A machine
surface added here never enters the graph, the asserted date freezes,
and a change to the vendored emitter reaches a copy that never runs it.

The workflow is generated by workflow() in @flashyos/directory rather
than hand-written, gates on the default branch resolved per run, and
commits with [skip ci] because a refresh is a record of what already
happened.

vendor-shiplog.mjs is re-vendored in the same commit: its bookkeeping
filter had never heard of "directory/1: refresh the fragment", so the
first refresh would have sealed as work under agent/unattributed.

Kind: feature

entries.title: Re-vendor check-directory.mjs: enforce what every edge type must carry
entries.detail:
The vendored checker had hand-written blocks for three of the sixteen edge
types and nothing for the other thirteen, so engaged without a basis,
delegatedTo without a scope and issued without a date all validated clean —
in thirty identical copies that agreed with each other perfectly.

It reads a requires table now, mirroring EDGE_REQUIRES in
@flashyos/directory, with one conditional: `declares` needs a role when it
names an agent and not when it names a machine surface. That split was
measured, not decided — across the estate all 88 agent declarations carry a
role and none of the 43 surface declarations do.

flashyos/tools/vendored-directory.test.mjs differentials this copy against
the package by verdict, and asserts every estate copy is byte-identical to
it. This repository's fragment passes the stricter checker unchanged.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Re-vendor shiplog: the hold retracts, and bookkeeping stays filtered [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
Two fixes in one copy, and this repository had neither.

The hold is applied at projection as well as at derivation, so it can retract
an entry already sealed public — the case claimyour.gold found, where an entry
quoting a bootstrap credential was served among 746 public entries. Visibility
is inside the digest, so re-deriving to change it is the restatement
append-only forbids; the entry now keeps its seal and stops being handed out.

And the bookkeeping filter tolerates the suffixes those subjects have grown.
It anchored on $ exactly, so adding [skip ci] to every emitted commit would
have started sealing each refresh as a shipped entry under agent/unattributed.

Holding is not remediation. A credential that reached a public history stays
burned until it is rotated.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Re-vendor shiplog: the hold can now retract an already-published entry [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
Visibility is inside an entry's digest, so an entry sealed public stays sealed
public — re-deriving it to change that is the restatement append-only forbids.
So a hold added afterwards changed nothing here: the entry kept being handed
out at the well-known URL.

claimyour.gold found the case. An entry explaining the removal of a bootstrap
credential quoted the token and the admin password verbatim, and was being
served among 746 public entries.

The fix applies the hold at projection as well as at derivation, so the record
keeps its seal and the served copy honours the hold: the entry stays in the
fragment, digest intact, counted, and simply stops being handed out.

It existed in flashyos's own root copy and in no other repository. Twenty-eight
vendored the version without it — including the one where the incident
happened. This is that copy, replaced.

Holding is still not remediation. A credential that reached a public history
stays burned until it is rotated.

Kind: fix

entries.title: An emitted record must not spend a deploy [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
The emitters commit a refreshed fragment on every push, and each of those is a
deployment. On 2026-08-31 the estate landed 594 commits on default branches and
321 of them — 54% — were emitters refreshing their own output. Vercel's build
rate limit is 100 a day across the account, so the record-keeping machinery was
consuming the whole estate's deploy budget three times over and starving the
pushes people actually made.

It was invisible everywhere. Each property sat a few revisions behind, gda.group
had stopped on 30 August, nothing was red. The one place it was written down was
a commit status on a dependabot PR nobody had opened: "Deployment rate limited —
retry in 24 hours."

[skip ci] is the marker Vercel and GitHub Actions both honour. The fragment
still reaches the domain on the next deploy a real push triggers, which is the
right cadence for a record of something that already happened.

This commit carries [vercel skip] rather than [skip ci] so CI still validates
it without spending one of the deploys it exists to save.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Re-vendor the backlog emitter: it can revise an item now
entries.detail:
`file` has taken `--wants` since the beginning and nothing could add them
afterwards, so every item filed across the estate — all of them filed without
wants — was permanently invisible to the matcher, which refuses an item that
names no `capabilitiesWanted`. A format whose central field is
write-once-at-creation is a format whose central field is empty.

`revise` changes everything about an item except its visibility. Promotion
stays a separate verb because it is a separate decision: it refuses anything
but a `person/` id, and folding it in would give a revision the power to
publish. Unmentioned fields are left alone — `close` is a revision too, and
clearing on absence would strip every want in the repository.

Copied byte-identical from flashyos rather than edited here. A stale vendored
file does not break; it disagrees, silently, about exactly the field somebody
has just added.

Kind: chore

entries.title: Close the backlog items this repository has since fixed
entries.detail:
These were filed from measurement — a signature citing an identity nothing
declared, a repository sealing a record and publishing no directory fragment
— and the measurement no longer finds them. An open item naming work that is
finished is a record that is wrong about the one thing a backlog is for.

Signed by the filing machine rather than by a person, and that asymmetry is
deliberate. Promotion publishes an organisation's intention on its behalf and
needs a named human; closure records that a measurement changed, makes
nothing visible to anyone new, and the identity that made the claim is the
honest one to withdraw it.

Left alone, these would have decayed in about ninety days. Ninety days of a
published backlog naming finished work is not a reason to wait.

Kind: chore

entries.title: shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it
Publish a directory/1 fragment, so this repository's signatures resolve
entries.detail:
Every sealed entry here carries `assertedBy: agent/<slug>-ci` and every filed
item carries `agent/<slug>-bot`, and nothing in the estate defined either. An
`assertedBy` naming an id nothing declares reads as provenance and carries
none, which is worse than leaving the field out — across the estate that was
2,478 edges citing identities that formally did not exist.

The repositories that already had a fragment each hand-wrote one around their
AAO charter. This repository has no charter, and neither will an outside
adopter of `shipped/1` on their first push, so the fragment comes from
`vendor-directory.mjs`: dependency-free, derived from the two config files
that already do the stamping, and validated here by the vendored checker.

It does not declare an organisation. `.shiplog/config.json` carries an `org`
field that adoption filled in with this repository's own slug, and in sixteen
repositories that names a company which does not exist. A repository is not
the authority for which organisation answers for it; defining one here to
raise a provenance number would put the fiction into the published graph. The
emitter says so on every run, and the gap is filed rather than papered over.

Kind: feat

entries.title: shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it
File the gaps this repository can prove about itself
entries.detail:
`backlog/1` was published by thirty repositories and empty in twenty-nine —
full distribution and nothing to distribute, which is worse than no adoption,
because a format every property emits and none fills teaches every reader that
the format is decorative.

The temptation was to write some intentions. That would be fabrication: an
agent inventing what an organisation intends is exactly what `promote()`
exists to prevent, and a backlog of plausible work nobody agreed to is worse
than an empty one.

So these are derived, not invented. Each item is a gap the estate survey
measures directly — a signature citing an identity nothing declares, a
repository sealing records and publishing no directory, a default branch that
is an agent's scratch branch — and each carries the evidence that establishes
it, because an item that says what to do without saying how anyone knows is an
instruction rather than a finding.

Filed private. Reaching public needs a named human to promote it, which is the
consent rule rather than an oversight.

Kind: feature

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FDosmV9fXV6oZ9NXe7PZ76

entries.title: shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it
Remove the second copy of Build OS; this repository is the site
entries.detail:
`vercel.json` deploys `site/` and nothing else here is built or served. The
`buildos/` directory was an exact, byte-for-byte copy of the standalone Build
OS repository — 54 source files, not deployed by this project, not built by it,
and with nothing anywhere to notice if the two ever disagreed.

They disagreed within an hour of somebody fixing dead imports in one of them,
which is the whole argument: a copy with no drift test does not fail, it
diverges, and the first person to find out is whoever debugs a fix that is
present in one repository and absent in the other.

One thing was worth carrying across and has been: this copy's `.gitignore`
recorded *why* it matches the whole `.env` family — `*.env` does not match
`.env.vercel`, and that gap is how a live AUTH_SECRET and six other credentials
reached a tracked file on 2026-08-23. The pattern was already right in the
standalone repository; the reason was only written here. It is written there
now.

The credential file was already untracked. **Removal is not rotation** — those
values are in the history of two repositories, they stay there, and they are
still to be rotated.

This also settles what this repository is asked for. It has no application
source now, so it owes no lint config and no test suite; it owes a deployed
site, which it has.

Kind: chore

entries.title: Carry the house rules, so an agent stops having to guess them
entries.detail:
Twenty of thirty-five repositories had no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, and an
agent with no repository doc guesses. Every avoidable mistake made across
this estate on 2026-08-30 happened in a repository without one — and each
was a fact that is true everywhere rather than a fact about that
repository:

  work pushed to `main` in eleven repositories whose default branch is not
  `main`, deploying nothing and read by nobody, with the push succeeding;

  a vendored emitter trusted after its source changed, so a privacy hold
  added that morning did nothing in sixteen repositories and published the
  entry it was meant to withhold;

  a copyright holder guessed as the studio on a client's site;

  measurements reported from a working copy while claiming to describe the
  branch that ships — twice, in two tools, by two agents, four hours apart.

None of that is repo-specific knowledge, and writing it thirty-five times
would drift the first time it changed. It is declared in
`tools/estate-house-rules.mjs` in flashyos and synced between two markers.
Everything outside the markers is this repository's own and is never
touched.

Where this file is new it says the repository is not yet described, which
is true. A generated description would be wrong and would read as
authoritative; admitting the gap is a task somebody can close in a minute.

Kind: docs

entries.title: Name a copyright holder, and stop granting what was never ours
entries.detail:
Two errors from the licence sweep of 2026-08-30, found by putting the
estate's licences in one register and comparing.

A LICENCE THAT NAMED NOBODY

Eleven repositories carried a bare Apache-2.0 text with no copyright line
at all. That is not a missing file — it is a file that answers the
question wrongly. It reads as a grant, and no reader can tell who made it
or whether they were entitled to. Every LICENSE now opens with the holder
and one line saying what the repository is.

AN OPEN LICENCE ON SOMEBODY ELSE'S PROPERTY

kopman-build and buildos are a construction firm's marketing site and the
application behind that engagement. Both carried AGPL-3.0-only, which
offers a client's own site to anyone willing to publish their changes.
Nobody decided that; it was the default that got reached for. Both are now
all rights reserved, held by Kopman Build, with a line saying ownership is
governed by the agreement between the firm and the studio rather than by
the file.

The same care had already been taken for marco.law an hour earlier and
then not taken here, which is the argument for a register rather than for
being more careful next time.

Eight further repositories moved from an unattributed Apache-2.0 to all
rights reserved: the org profile, the Terraform that can delete
production, three brand properties and the three Life repositories.
flashy-sdk is among them and its package.json already said UNLICENSED —
the LICENSE file had been contradicting its own manifest.

`tools/estate-licences.mjs` in flashyos is now the one declaration, and it
reports a checkout and a default branch separately, because conflating
those is the mistake this estate's tooling keeps making.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Close the gap that let a secret reach a tracked file, and scan for the next one
entries.detail:
The committed AUTH_SECRET has already been removed on this branch. What had
not been fixed is the reason it got in: `.gitignore` listed `*.env`, which
matches a file ending in `.env` and does not match `.env.vercel`. The pattern
is now `.env.*` with an escape for `.env.example`, so the family is covered
rather than one spelling of it.

Secret scanning arrives with it — vendored byte-identical across the estate,
scanning the working tree rather than history so it blocks the next committed
secret without failing forever on a historical value pending rotation.
Verified clean against this branch before pushing, so it arrives green.

The disclosed value is still disclosed. Removal from the tree is not rotation:
AUTH_SECRET remains in this repository's history and must be rotated, and
anything signed with it treated as compromised.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BEaXzktRU5ZPe3R2NY7CKD

entries.title: Declare a licence: AGPL-3.0-only
entries.detail:
Source with no licence file is all rights reserved by default. Nobody may
legally use, fork or embed it — including a future acquirer’s diligence team,
and including anyone who reads this estate’s claim to publish an open
organisational protocol and goes looking for the source.

AGPL-3.0-only, which is what the estate applies to anything hosted: a hosted
fork must publish its changes. The spec and the published clients stay
Apache-2.0 so that anyone may embed them, including in closed software.

The full text ships rather than only a field, because a repository that names
a licence and does not carry it makes a claim a reader cannot check.

entries.detail:
A stale copy fails silently and in the dangerous direction: it does not know
about rules added since it was vendored, so it ignores them rather than

Kind: fix

entries.title: Fail loudly on a fragment that exists and cannot be parsed
entries.detail:
The emitter treated an unparseable fragment as an absent one and built a head
over whatever else it could read. A conflicted fragment produced a
valid-looking head over nothing.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Re-emit the log and its checkpoint after rebase
entries.detail: Kind: chore

entries.title: Adopt checkpoint/1 — a tree head over what this repository seals
entries.detail:
An RFC 6962 Merkle root over the sealed claims already published here, served
beside them. Anyone holding the fragments can recompute it and see whether the
record still describes what it said it did.

The head is deliberately unsigned. A signature over a root computed and checked
by the same party is ceremony without a property — what makes history provably
append-only is a witness who is not us, and that is not built. The root catches
drift and after-the-fact edits, and nothing here claims more.

It is refreshed by the shiplog workflow rather than its own, so the head and
the log it commits to always move in one commit. A separate workflow would
leave a window in which the published root and the published record disagree,
and a reader hitting that window sees a forged-looking estate.

Kind: feature

entries.title: Re-vendor the emitter, and publish this log
entries.detail:
The vendored copy here predated four changes: an emit that unions rather
than replaces, a per-entry privacy hold, a guard that stops an agent's
commits being filed under a person, and a filter for this format's own
refresh commits.

A stale vendored copy does not fail. It disagrees with the source about
what it was told to do — which is how a hold added this morning did
nothing in sixteen repositories and marked the held entry public.
estate-hygiene now compares every vendor-*.mjs byte-for-byte against the
package it came from, and this repository was one of nine it caught.

visibility is public. Everything derived has been private since adoption;
this is the decision that makes it a changelog anyone can read.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Map the estate's commit addresses to who they belong to
entries.detail:
`authors` was empty and `defaultAuthor` filed every entry under one identity,
so this log looked fully attributed while agent-authored commits were recorded
as the person named as the default.

The map is declared once in flashyos `tools/estate-authors.mjs` and synced
here. Five addresses are left unmapped on purpose, each with a stated reason.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Stop pinning the shiplog and backlog workflows to a branch name
entries.detail:
Each workflow triggered on `branches: ['<the default branch at adoption>']`.
Eleven repositories in this estate have a `claude/*` branch as their GitHub
default; renaming one to `main` is the right thing to do and would have stopped
its workflow firing. Nothing would have failed — the fragment would simply have
stopped advancing, and a stale changelog reads exactly like a current one.

The trigger now matches any push and the job is gated on
`github.ref_name == github.event.repository.default_branch`, resolved per run,
so a rename is survived rather than discovered. `branch` is dropped from the
config: nothing read it, and a stored branch name is a snapshot of something
that changes.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Reclassify the log against the convention this estate writes in
entries.detail:
The derived log was classified only by conventional-commit prefixes, and
this repository writes declarative English. Unclassified went from 76%
to 8% by reading the estate's declared imperative lexicon, looking
past a project prefix to the verb behind it, and dropping merges of
another branch into this line — which are not things that shipped.

Nothing is published: entries remain private and the served copy is the
public projection.

Kind: infra

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FDosmV9fXV6oZ9NXe7PZ76

entries.title: Point the workflows at the branch this repository actually defaults to
entries.detail:
Adoption wrote `main`, and this repository has no `main` — its remote
HEAD is a branch named after the change that created it. A workflow
written for a branch that does not exist is the silent kind of broken:
it is present, it reads correctly, and it never fires.

Fixed in the adopt command too, which now asks the remote for its HEAD
when the local refs say nothing and neither main nor master was fetched.

entries.title: Adopt backlog/1 and shipped/1
entries.detail:
This repository now publishes the two tenses the estate records: what it
intends, and what it shipped. Both are emitted by a dependency-free
vendored script, so nothing here gains a toolchain it did not have.

Nothing is published by this commit. Backlog items are filed private and
reach the served fragment only when a named human promotes one; shipped
entries land private until someone changes one field in
.shiplog/config.json. The served copy is the public projection and the
emitter writes it, so a private record cannot reach a URL through a
forgotten copy step.

Derived 24 entries from this repository's own history, every seal
recomputed. Org org/kopman-build, served at none.

entries.title: Phase 5 — Video-to-quote AI, Marketplace, Cost Intelligence, White-label
entries.detail:
Video-to-Quote Pipeline:
- Presigned R2 upload for video files (500MB cap, 15min TTL)
- Frame extraction worker dispatch (Railway service, AWS Batch in Phase 6)
- Claude Vision analysis of up to 20 keyframes — rooms identified, condition notes,
  per-line-item confidence levels, flagged issues, recommended follow-up
- Secure frame-extraction webhook receiver (shared secret auth)
- Full job lifecycle: uploading → extracting → analyzing → complete/failed

Cost Intelligence Engine:
- Historical benchmark queries (P25/avg/P75 contract value per project type)
- Quote audit: flags quotes >40% above/below tenant's own historical average
- AI margin report (Haiku) — natural language executive summary per period

Marketplace (multi-firm lead routing):
- Seller side: list overflow leads with AI-generated PII-free summary, set price
- Buyer side: browse available leads by city/type/price, claim via Stripe payment
- Platform commission (10%) via Stripe Connect application_fee_amount
- Contact info released only after payment confirmed via webhook
- Lead TTL: 72h auto-expiry (pg_cron snippet in migration)
- Revenue tracking: leads sold, gross/net revenue per origin tenant

White-label (Enterprise):
- Custom domain, brand name, primary color, logo, favicon, custom CSS
- hideBuiltWith flag, supportEmail override
- brandTokens endpoint for CSS variable injection
- Gated behind assertFeatureAccess("white_label") → Enterprise plan only

DB Phase 5 schema + migration:
- marketplace_profiles, marketplace_leads, lead_purchases
- video_quote_jobs (with RLS)
- whitelabel_configs
- Grants + pg_cron lead expiry snippet

entries.title: Phase 4 — Stripe SaaS billing + Connect + tenant onboarding
entries.detail:
Stripe SaaS Billing:
- Three plans: Starter ($99), Growth ($299), Enterprise ($999/mo)
- Checkout session creation with 14-day trial
- Customer Portal for self-serve plan changes / cancellation
- Webhook handler: checkout.session.completed, subscription.updated/deleted, payment_failed
